column4: There is a cognitive trap in changing our minds. If we don’t perceive a need to change our minds, then why would we ever open our eyes to look for change? Again, back to the poison analogy, if you cannot perceive that the poison is killing you, why would you stop consuming it?

column4: Some people believe that a person just must hit ‘rock-bottom’, then they will look at their lives and decide to change. Experience and psychology tell us we humans are more complex. There are many theories related to behavior change in the study of psychology, one highly regarded theory is the **Transtheoretical Model of Change** Developed in the late 1970s by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente **\\[1\\].**
column5: Some believe that if a person just reaches “rock bottom,” they will take a hard look at their life and decide to change. Experience and psychology teach us that we humans are more complicated. Psychological research includes many theories of behavior change, and among the most highly regarded is the **Transtheoretical Model of Behavior Change**, developed in the late 1970s by James Prochaska and Carlo DiClemente **[1].**

column4: People may go through a cycle of six stages for change:
column5: People may go through a six-stage cycle toward change:

column4: 1.  Precontemplation: There is no intention to change.
column5: 1.  Precontemplation: No intention to change.

column4: 2.  Contemplation: There is an intention to change in the near future.
column5: 2.  Contemplation: Intention to change in the near future.

column4: 3.  Preparation: Some steps have been taken to change.
column5: 3.  Preparation: Taking some steps toward change.

column4: 4.  Action: The behavior has been changed for a short time.
column5: 4.  Action: Behavior has changed for a short period.

column4: 5.  Maintenance: The behavior has been changed and continues to be maintained.
column5: 5.  Maintenance: Behavior has changed and is being maintained.

column4: 6.  Termination: There is no desire to return to the previous behavior.
column5: 6.  Termination: No desire to return to the previous behavior.

column4: There is no set length of time for how long any stage may take. Some people with respect to certain issues in their lives never meaningfully progress through the stages. In other instances, we can progress from stage 1 to 6 very expediently.
column5: There is no set length for how long each stage takes. For certain life challenges, some people do not progress meaningfully through the stages. In other instances, they may move very quickly from stage 1 to 6.

column5: Though the idea that hitting rock bottom is a sure prerequisite for change is close to a myth, God can use sorrow to work on our hearts。 God uses sorrow to lead us to repentance。 He gives us a conviction of sin regarding our deeds, our lives, and the state of our hearts, opening our eyes to show us how completely and utterly we need God。

column4: Godly sorrow, or <u>the experience of sadness or distress that leads to a *metanoia*</u>, is not the same thing worldly sorrow. Worldly sorrow is the same experience of sadness or distress, but the world offers no hope, only the relief and promise of death.
column5: Godly sorrow, or the <u>experience of sorrow or distress that leads to *metanoia*</u>, is not the same as the sorrow of this world。 In worldly sorrow, the experience of sorrow or distress itself is the same, but the world gives no hope; what remains is only the promise of alleviation and of death。

column4: Sorrow is also different from suffering and grief.
column5: Sorrow is different from suffering and grief as well。

column4: Suffering is the endurance of pain-physical, emotional, mental, or spiritual-especially when prolonged or intense.
column5: Suffering is to endure pain—physical, emotional, mental, and also spiritual—especially when it is prolonged or intense.

column4: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially relational or existential.
column5: Grief is a multifaceted emotional response to significant personal loss, especially losses involving relationships or existence。

column4: Sorrow, suffering, and grief are closely related ideas. In the human condition we will experience all three, we can learn and grow through all three, but God will not bring about death and destruction in our lives to teach us.
column5: Sorrow, suffering, and lament are concepts that are closely related to one another. Given the human condition, we experience all three, and through all three we can learn and grow; however, God does not bring death and destruction into our lives in order to teach us.

column4: The scriptures say every good and perfect gift is from God above (James 1:17). He is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow will cause discomfort, but His discipline is just and loving. Just as a good father would not intentionally break his child’s arm to ‘teach him a lesson’, God will not inflict sickness or disease on His children to teach us.
column5: The Bible says that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, from God (James 1:17). God is a good Father who knows how to give good gifts to His children (Matthew 7:11). Godly sorrow brings discomfort, but God’s discipline is just and full of love. Just as a good father would not deliberately break his child’s arm “to teach a lesson,” God does not afflict His children with sickness or disease in order to teach us.

column4: ### Example of Worldly Sorrow vs Godly Sorrow
column5: ### Examples of Worldly Sorrow and Godly Sorrow

column4: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick, and he intentionally hit her, causing her to cry and leaving a red mark.
column5: A three-year-old boy was playing in the yard with his two-year-old sister. He was playing with a stick and intentionally hit her; she cried, and it left a red mark.

column4: Their father hearing the commotion investigated and when he learned what his son did took the stick, broke it in half and tossed it away. He sent his son inside to think about what did and comforted his daughter.
column5: Hearing the commotion, their father came to check, and when he learned what his son had done, he took the stick, snapped it in two, and threw it away. He sent his son inside to think about what he had done and comforted his daughter.

column4: The father coming inside to deal with his son found him crying. Asking him why he was crying his son said, “because you broke my stick”.
column5: When the father came inside to deal with his son, he found him crying. When he asked why he was crying, the boy said, “Because you broke my stick.”

column4: The father’s reply was, “I’m sad that you are more concerned about your stick than you are about your sister who you hurt” and sent him back to his room for more reflection.
column5: The father replied, “It makes me sad that you’re more concerned about your stick than about your sister whom you hurt,” and sent him back to his room to think further.

column4: A few minutes later his son came back out and apologized. He said he was still sad because dad has broken his stick, and because he had hit his sister.
column5: A few minutes later, the boy came back and apologized. He said he was still sad that Dad had broken his stick, and he was also sad that he had hit his sister.

column4: **Progress!**
column5: **Progress!**

column4: In this example the boy experienced both worldly sorrow, for his lost stick, and then eventually godly sorrow, for his hurt sister.
column5: In this example, the boy experienced worldly sorrow over the stick he lost, and eventually he also experienced godly sorrow over the sister he had hurt.

column4: Godly sorrow and God’s goodness are connected. God is a good father that will let us experience the consequences of our actions but will still stand beside us as we walk through those consequences.
column5: Godly sorrow is tied to God’s goodness. God is a good Father who allows us to experience the consequences of our actions, yet even as we walk through those consequences, He stands with us.

column4: God's unrelenting goodness, to be willing to redeem us and restore us if we come to Him is a positive agent in our path of repentance. His goodness isn’t that we continue in sin, but that despite our sin He makes a way for us to be redeemed and experience His salvation.
column5: God’s unceasing goodness—His will to redeem and restore us if we come to Him—is a positive driving force on our path of repentance. God’s goodness does not mean that we remain in sin; rather, despite our sin, He provides a way for us to be redeemed and to experience His salvation.

column4: In our subsequent studies on the Holy Spirit and on sanctification, we will see in greater depth how the Spirit calls and transforms the hearts of men. Let's look at one such example, the story of King David and his example of repentance.
column5: In the following study on the Holy Spirit and sanctification, we will look more deeply at how the Holy Spirit calls and transforms the human heart。As a first example, let us look at the story of King David and his model of repentance。

column4: ### David’s Example of Repentance
column5: ### David’s Model of Repentance

column4: Perhaps no account in the scriptures has a richer example of repentance than the story of King David’s sin found in 2 Samuel 11-12. It begins with King David remaining in Jerusalem instead of going to battle, where he sees Bathsheba bathing. Despite knowing she is the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David sends for her, and they have an affair, resulting in Bathsheba's pregnancy.
column5: Perhaps no story in the Bible shows a model of repentance so richly as the account of King David’s sin recorded in 2 Samuel 11–12。The narrative begins when King David, who stayed in Jerusalem instead of going out to battle, saw Bathsheba bathing。Even though he knew she was the wife of Uriah, one of his loyal soldiers, David summoned her and slept with her, and as a result Bathsheba conceived。

column4: To cover his actions, David recalls Uriah from the battlefield, hoping he will spend time with Bathsheba and appear to be the child's father. However, Uriah, out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers, refuses to go to his home with Bethsheba. David then arranges for Uriah to be sent to the front lines where he is ultimately killed in battle. After Uriah's death, David hastily marries Bathsheba to cover up the pregnancy.

column4: The Lord is displeased with David's actions and sends the prophet Nathan to confront him. When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, "*I have sinned against the Lord*" (2 Samuel 12:13). David did not try to justify or excuse his actions. This confession was the first step in his repentance, acknowledging his wrongdoing directly to God.
column5: The Lord was displeased with David’s actions and sent the prophet Nathan to rebuke him。When confronted by the prophet, David immediately admitted, 「*I have sinned against the Lord*」 （2 Samuel 12:13）。David did not justify his actions or make excuses。この告白は、神に直接自分の過ちを認めるという、彼の悔い改めの第一歩でした。

column4: In Psalm 51, David’s words, “*For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me,*” show his complete ownership of his actions. He expresses grief not only for the sin itself but also for how it offended God, saying, “*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*” David displayed "*a broken and contrite heart,*" an essential part of true repentance (Psalms 51:17). This sorrow wasn’t superficial; he deeply grieved over the sin he committed and the hurt it caused. This depth of remorse was a sign that he wanted not only forgiveness but a changed heart.
column5: In Psalm 51, David says, 「*I know my transgressions; my sin is always before me，*」 fully owning his actions。He laments not only the sin itself but also how it has offended God, saying, 「*Against you, you only, have I sinned.*」 David showed a 「*broken and contrite heart*」 essential to true repentance（Psalm 51:17）。This sorrow was not superficial。He deeply grieved the sin he had committed and the pain it caused。This deep contrition was a sign that he sought not just forgiveness but a transformed heart。

column4: David asked God to “*Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me”* (Psalms 51:10). He sought an inner transformation that would prevent him from repeating the same mistakes. Rather than just apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, saying, “*Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow*” (Psalms 51:7). He recognized that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy.
column5: David asked God, 「*Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me*」 （Psalm 51:10）。He sought an inner change that would keep him from repeating the same failures。Rather than merely apologizing, David pleaded with God to cleanse him, 「*Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow*」 （Psalm 51:7）。He acknowledged that only God could purify his heart and restore his joy。

column4: David’s desire to be renewed spiritually reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways moving forward. His request for a “*willing spirit*” (Psalms 51:12) demonstrates his hope to be aligned with God in every part of his life.
column5: David’s desire to be spiritually renewed reflects a genuine commitment to walk in God’s ways going forward。His request for a 「*willing spirit*」 （Psalm 51:12） shows his desire to be aligned with God in every area of life。

column4: Although God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child and he was very sick. David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God to spare the child, but when the child died, David accepted it (2 Samuel 12:15-23).
column5: Even though God put away David’s sin, the Lord struck the child, and the child became gravely ill。David fasted, prayed, and pleaded with God for the child to live, but when the child died, David accepted it（2 Samuel 12:15-23）。

column4: In Psalm 51 we find a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgressions. David’s decision to write down his plea for mercy, creating one of the Bible’s most enduring psalms, shows his willingness to be transparent about his sin and God’s forgiveness. This psalm became a testimony of repentance and restoration for others to learn from, memorializing his journey from guilt to grace.
column5: In Psalm 51 we see both a personal prayer of repentance and a public acknowledgment of his transgression。David’s recording of his plea for mercy, which produced one of the most enduring psalms in Scripture, shows his willingness to be candid about his sin and God’s forgiveness。This psalm stands as a testimony of repentance and restoration from which others can learn, commemorating his journey from guilt to grace。

column4: David’s repentance journey was not simply about feeling sorry; it was a profound change in his heart and life. Through confession, acceptance, and the heart transformation inscribed in Psalm 51, David memorialized his sin as a lesson on God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the Bible's most significant examples of genuine repentance.
column5: David’s journey of repentance was not merely feeling sorry; it was a profound change of heart and way of life。Through the confession, acceptance, and transformation of heart inscribed in Psalm 51, David recorded his sin as a lesson about God’s mercy, repentance, and the possibility of restoration, making his story one of the most important biblical examples of genuine repentance。
